\section{Popularity ranking, exposure balancing and the length of
search: a pre-registered simulation of sequential discovery in synthetic
two-sided matching
markets}\label{popularity-ranking-exposure-balancing-and-the-length-of-search-a-pre-registered-simulation-of-sequential-discovery-in-synthetic-two-sided-matching-markets}

\textbf{Status.} Independent research manuscript, preprint draft, not
peer-reviewed. Version 1.0, 2026-11-25. The title was approved by the
owner on 2026-11-25 (decision D-024); the working title was \emph{Can
optimal matching leave more people unhappy?}

\subsection{Author and affiliation
metadata}\label{author-and-affiliation-metadata}

Mohamed Bechir Kefi. Independent researcher; no institutional
affiliation.

AI assistance: an AI system (Claude, Anthropic) was used as a research
and development assistant for code, analysis and drafting under the
author's direction. It is not an author. The author is responsible for
the content.

\subsection{Abstract}\label{abstract}

Partner-search platforms decide which candidates each participant sees.
We ask how such exposure policies change match outcomes when preferences
are reciprocal and heterogeneous, using fully synthetic two-sided
markets. Agents on two sides (200 on the short side, imbalance ratio 1.0
to 1.5) hold Gaussian common-plus-idiosyncratic utilities with
preference correlation 0, 0.5 or 0.9. In sequential discovery, every
unmatched agent sees a slate of five candidates per round, chosen at
random (baseline), by observed like rate (popularity) or by like rate
under a per-round exposure cap (exposure-balanced). The estimand, frozen
before the confirmatory runs, is the equal-weight mean over nine design
cells of the paired difference in mean agent welfare after 40 rounds, on
270 market instances. Popularity ranking raised welfare by 0.0219 (95\%
CI 0.0207 to 0.0231; Holm-adjusted p = 0.0002), but the pre-registered
sensitivity analysis found the sign reversed at 10 and 20 rounds
(-0.4081 and -0.2824), so the result is reported as not robust to the
horizon. Exposure-balanced ranking was equivalent to random exposure
within a margin of 0.01 (estimate 0.0004, 90\% CI -0.0005 to 0.0013).
Centralized deferred acceptance exceeded random discovery by 0.0963, and
the welfare-maximizing assignment left 231 more blocking pairs per 100
agents than deferred acceptance. Exploratory diagnostics added after the
confirmatory analysis show that popularity ranking was still forming
matches at round 40, when random exposure had almost always stopped, so
the primary estimate is a fixed-horizon quantity. All findings concern a
stylized simulation, not real people or platforms; a registered
metric-definition check was not run.

\subsection{Keywords}\label{keywords}

two-sided matching; exposure; ranking policies; sequential search;
deferred acceptance; pre-registered simulation

\subsection{1. Introduction}\label{introduction}

Many platforms that help people find partners, collaborators or
counterparts do not assign matches. They decide who sees whom, and
participants then choose among the candidates they are shown. Because
attention is scarce and every participant can match only once, the
exposure policy can matter: it may change who is matched, how good those
matches are for each side, and how unequally attention is spread.
Exposure as a resource that rankings allocate has been studied as a
fairness problem in ranking (Singh and Joachims 2018), and ranking by
relevance alone has been argued to be suboptimal in matching markets
with capacity limits (Su, Bayoumi and Joachims 2021, preprint).
Classical matching theory, in contrast, studies centralized mechanisms
such as deferred acceptance (Gale and Shapley 1962).

This project asks: \emph{how do ranking and exposure policies alter
match outcomes under heterogeneous preferences?} It answers only inside
an explicit synthetic model. Every participant is simulated; nothing
here describes real people, protected attributes or the internals of any
platform.

The confirmatory question (EXP-001) is whether two simple slate
policies, popularity ranking and exposure-balanced ranking, change mean
agent welfare relative to random exposure. A secondary experiment
(EXP-002) places centralized references, deferred acceptance and a
utilitarian assignment, on the same markets. A sensitivity experiment
(EXP-003) was registered to test whether the main result survives
changes in pickiness, horizon and welfare definition. The hypotheses
were nondirectional because the sources reviewed did not fix a sign for
this model.

The contributions are modest and stated precisely:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  A small, open and fully reproducible simulation that runs three slate
  policies and three centralized mechanisms on the same synthetic market
  instances with common random numbers, varying side imbalance and
  preference correlation jointly.
\item
  A confirmatory test frozen before execution, with a pre-registered
  invalidation rule, and its result reported under that rule: a positive
  welfare effect of popularity ranking at the primary horizon that is
  not robust to shorter horizons, and an equivalence-to-zero result for
  exposure-balanced ranking at a margin of 0.01.
\item
  A complete account of what was not done or did not hold, including a
  registered sensitivity analysis that was not run, and exploratory
  diagnostics that qualify the confirmatory reading.
\end{enumerate}

No novelty relative to the literature is claimed; the literature search
was short and not systematic (Section 2).

\subsection{2. Related work}\label{related-work}

The sources below were opened on 2026-11-24 at the level stated; nothing
is cited for content beyond that level
(\texttt{research/literature\_review.md}).

\textbf{Stable matching.} Deferred acceptance produces a stable matching
(Gale and Shapley 1962), and proposer optimality among stable matchings
is standard background (Roth 1982). For both, only bibliographic
metadata were verified; the facts used here rest on the standard
definitions and on this project's tests, which check stability against
brute-force enumeration on small markets. Ashlagi, Kanoria and Leshno
(2017; abstract verified) report that in random markets even a slight
imbalance gives an essentially unique stable matching in which the short
side does much better; this motivates varying the imbalance ratio.

\textbf{Platform search.} Kanoria and Saban (2021; abstract verified)
study how a platform can facilitate search by restricting search
actions, in a model with costly search. Hitsch, Hortacsu and Ariely
(2010; abstract verified) compare observed online-dating matches with
predictions from a stable-matching model and discuss search frictions as
one explanation for discrepancies. This project makes no empirical claim
about any platform and uses these works only for framing.

\textbf{Exposure and ranking in matching markets.} Singh and Joachims
(2018; abstract verified) treat exposure as the quantity a ranking
allocates and propose fairness constraints on it. Su, Bayoumi and
Joachims (2021; abstract verified; preprint) argue that ranking by local
relevance is suboptimal in matching markets with capacity constraints.
Tomita and Yokoyama (2024; abstract verified; arXiv comments state
acceptance at RecSys 2024) study envy-freeness of recommendation
opportunities in reciprocal recommendation and a trade-off between
expected matches and fairness.

\textbf{Relation to this work.} This study is neither a replication nor
an extension of any of these models. It is a small, pre-registered
simulation of three deliberately simple slate policies. The policies are
stylized and are not reproductions of any deployed algorithm or of the
methods in the cited papers.

\subsection{3. Background and formal
model}\label{background-and-formal-model}

\textbf{Population.} Two sides A and B, with \textbar A\textbar{} = n\_A
= 200 and \textbar B\textbar{} = n\_B = round(r n\_A), imbalance ratio r
in \{1.0, 1.1, 1.5\}; B is the long side. Each agent x has a latent
quality q\_x drawn from N(0, 1). The utility of agent i for agent j on
the other side is

u\_ij = sqrt(rho) q\_j + sqrt(1 - rho) e\_ij, with e\_ij drawn from N(0,
1),

so for two viewers the correlation of their utilities over candidates is
rho in \{0, 0.5, 0.9\}. Rho = 0 gives idiosyncratic tastes; rho near 1
gives near-consensus tastes. Both sides draw utilities independently
with the same rho.

\textbf{Satisfaction and acceptability.} The satisfaction of i with j is
the rank percentile s\_ij = 1 - (rank\_i(j) - 1)/(m\_i - 1), where
rank\_i(j) is j's rank in i's strict ordering of the whole other side,
of size m\_i. Agent i finds j acceptable when u\_ij is at least the
theta-quantile of i's utilities; the primary pickiness is theta = 0.5.
Capacity is one on both sides and unmatched agents have satisfaction 0.

\textbf{Sequential discovery.} In each round t = 1, \ldots, T (primary T
= 40), every unmatched agent on both sides is shown a slate of up to k =
5 unmatched candidates it has not seen before; viewers are processed in
a seeded random order. Viewer i likes j if j is acceptable to i. A pair
becomes a mutual like once both have liked each other, in any rounds. At
the end of each round, new mutual likes are resolved greedily in
decreasing order of s\_ij + s\_ji, and matched agents leave. Exposure
e\_j counts the slates in which j appeared. The three policies are:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  RANDOM (baseline): a uniform draw from the eligible candidates.
\item
  POPULARITY: candidates sorted by the smoothed like rate p\_j = (L\_j +
  1)/(e\_j + 2), where L\_j counts likes received; ties are broken by
  one uniform random key per candidate per round, shared by all viewers
  in that round (amendment F2 of the frozen protocol).
\item
  EXPOSURE\_BALANCED: the same score, but in each round no candidate may
  appear in more than c = ceil((1 + delta) k V / C) slates, with V the
  number of viewers, C the number of eligible candidates and delta =
  0.5. If fewer than k candidates remain under the cap, the slate is
  shorter.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Centralized references.} DA\_A and DA\_B are deferred acceptance
with side A or side B proposing, over lists truncated to acceptable
partners. MAXW maximizes the sum over matched pairs of s\_ij + s\_ji
among mutually acceptable pairs (rectangular linear assignment). These
use full preference information and are references, not deployable
discovery policies.

\textbf{Metrics.} The primary metric is mean agent welfare W = (1/(n\_A
+ n\_B)) times the sum over all agents of their satisfaction, with
unmatched agents at 0; it is unitless in {[}0, 1{]}. Secondary metrics
are the unmatched fraction U (the share of all agents left unmatched),
mutual satisfaction M (the mean over matched pairs of min(s\_ij,
s\_ji)), the Gini coefficient of exposure per side, blocking pairs per
100 agents (a pair count that is not bounded by 100), and W by side and
by quality quartile. Because U is the unmatched share of all agents, W
can be written as W = (1 - U) Q, where Q is the mean satisfaction of
matched agents; this identity is used in the exploratory analysis of
Section 5.4.

\textbf{Estimand.} For a policy P and market instance m, D\_P(m) =
W\_P(m) - W\_RANDOM(m) on the same instance. The estimand is theta\_P,
the equal-weight mean over the nine (r, rho) cells of E{[}D\_P
\textbar{} cell{]}.

\textbf{Complexity.} A sequential run costs O(T (n\_A + n\_B) k) slate
operations plus scoring; MAXW solves one rectangular assignment of at
most 200 by 300. The measured run bodies were short (Section 4.5).

\subsection{4. Methods}\label{methods}

\subsubsection{4.1 Design and
registration}\label{design-and-registration}

The protocol (\texttt{research/protocol.md} and one protocol per
experiment) was drafted before any run, amended on the basis of an
exploratory full-size pilot, and frozen by the owner on 2026-11-24 with
SHA-256 hashes of every protocol and confirmatory configuration recorded
in \texttt{research/freeze.json}. The pre-freeze pilot values of the
primary contrast were seen before the freeze and are disclosed in the
freeze record (decision C4): for POPULARITY, -0.2917 at T = 20 over nine
cells and 0.0178 at T = 40 on the corner cells; for EXPOSURE\_BALANCED,
0.0034 and 0.005. The owner chose the primary horizon T = 40 and the
shared tie key with these values available, so the primary horizon is
the one at which POPULARITY had turned positive in the pilot. The
recorded purpose of the longer horizon (amendment F1) was to let all
arms stop matching; Section 5.4 shows that this was not achieved for
POPULARITY. A runtime guard refuses any confirmatory configuration whose
hash does not match the freeze record.

\textbf{Experimental unit and pairing.} The unit is one market instance
(one draw of qualities and utilities). Agents inside an instance are
never treated as independent. Thirty instances per cell were drawn from
the root seed 20261124 through numpy \texttt{SeedSequence} spawning;
every arm runs on the same instance with common random numbers, and the
viewer-order and tie-break streams are shared across arms that consume
them identically.

\subsubsection{4.2 Hypotheses and decision
rules}\label{hypotheses-and-decision-rules}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{EXP-001 (confirmatory).} For P in \{POPULARITY,
  EXPOSURE\_BALANCED\}, H0\_P: theta\_P = 0 against H1\_P: theta\_P !=
  0, Holm correction over the two contrasts, familywise alpha 0.05. A
  Holm-adjusted p of at least 0.05 means H1\_P is not supported.
  Equivalence is claimed only if the 90\% CI of theta\_P lies inside
  (-0.01, 0.01), the smallest effect size of interest.
\item
  \textbf{EXP-002 (secondary, no multiplicity protection).} H\_a: the
  equal-weight mean of W(DA\_A) - W(RANDOM) differs from 0. H\_b: the
  equal-weight mean of blocking pairs per 100 agents, MAXW minus DA\_A,
  differs from 0. A 95\% CI containing 0 means not supported. Zero
  blocking pairs for DA is an invariant whose failure would indicate a
  bug.
\item
  \textbf{EXP-003 (sensitivity).} Invalidation criterion, fixed in
  advance: if theta\_P under any S2 or S3 setting has the opposite sign
  of the EXP-001 estimate with a 95\% CI excluding 0, the EXP-001 result
  for P is reported as not robust. S1 is reported but is not part of the
  criterion.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{4.3 Statistical analysis}\label{statistical-analysis}

Per-cell paired mean differences carry 95\% percentile bootstrap CIs
over instances (10,000 resamples). The pooled theta\_P carries 95\% and
90\% stratified bootstrap CIs (instances resampled within each cell).
EXP-001 p-values come from a stratified paired sign-flip randomization
test with 10,000 draws, so the smallest attainable p-value is 1/10,001;
tests are limited to the EXP-001 family (protocol section 8). Effect
sizes are mean differences in welfare units and the standardized paired
effect dz. The analysis code for EXP-002 and EXP-003 was committed
before any confirmatory output existed (decision D-017).

\subsubsection{4.4 Exploratory analyses added in
M4}\label{exploratory-analyses-added-in-m4}

After the confirmatory results were known, three exploratory analyses
were run to inspect competing explanations. They are labelled
exploratory wherever they appear, test no hypothesis and change no
frozen verdict (decision D-021).

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{E1, horizon saturation} (journal J-0014): from the stored
  per-round match counts of the committed runs, the share of instances
  with at least one new match in the last 10 rounds of the horizon.
\item
  \textbf{E2, unmatched-value sweep} (J-0014): because W counts an
  unmatched agent as 0 and U is the unmatched share of all agents, the
  welfare with a constant unmatched value v is exactly W + vU. The
  contrast is reported over the whole range v in \{0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75,
  1\} together with the break-even value at which its sign would change.
  This is not the registered S3, which is recorded as not run and whose
  parameters are not chosen after the data (D-019); it uses one constant
  value for every agent and does not change the satisfaction scale.
\item
  \textbf{E3, decomposition} (J-0014): paired differences in the matched
  share 1 - U and in Q = W/(1 - U), the mean satisfaction of matched
  agents.
\item
  \textbf{E4, horizon-extension probe} (J-0015): a new exploratory run
  on a fresh root seed (505), all nine cells, 10 instances per cell, the
  three sequential arms, at T = 40, 80 and 160 (810 runs).
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{4.5 Implementation, verification and
resources}\label{implementation-verification-and-resources}

The simulator is the Python package \texttt{match\_lab} 0.2.0 (Python
3.12.1, numpy 2.3.5, scipy 1.16.3, dependencies locked). The test suite
(103 tests before the confirmatory runs) covers deferred acceptance on
hand-computed examples, zero blocking pairs for DA against brute-force
enumeration, MAXW against brute force, metric values on hand-computed
markets, no duplicate matches, capacity one, empty pools, determinism
for a fixed seed and the freeze guard. Before the confirmatory runs, an
independent naive recomputation of W, U, M and blocking pairs agreed
exactly with the stored metrics on eight runs (J-0009). Every
confirmatory run passed the validity checks at export and import. The
runs used an Apple M1 Pro under \texttt{nice} on a shared machine:
EXP-001 took 255.2 s of wall clock, EXP-002 13.6 s and EXP-003 392.3 s,
against a frozen budget of 30 minutes per experiment. Runtimes are
diagnostics only; no result depends on them.

\subsubsection{4.6 Deviations and owner
decisions}\label{deviations-and-owner-decisions}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{EXP-003 S3 not run.} S3 was specified as a reanalysis of
  EXP-001 raw outputs, but those outputs store per-run metrics, not
  matchings or utilities, and the frozen text does not fix how utility
  is standardized or how the threshold's satisfaction is defined. The
  owner recorded S3 as not run, a documented failure, with no parameters
  chosen after the data (D-018, D-019).
\item
  \textbf{Provenance revision.} The confirmatory runs used revision
  cfc90d0, not the frozen-content revision 88f3438; the difference is
  records, the EXP-002 and EXP-003 analysis module, the CLI, tests and
  the restriction of p-values to EXP-001. No simulation, metric or
  statistics code changed, and every frozen hash still matches (D-017).
\item
  \textbf{Analysis command.} The protocol's reproduction command
  produces a generic per-file report that cannot pair EXP-002 arms with
  the EXP-001 RANDOM arm; the frozen contrasts are computed by a
  separate \texttt{analyze} command written before any confirmatory
  output.
\item
  \textbf{Unscheduled run.} During the freeze session an old test
  executed the EXP-001 configuration once by accident. Its outputs were
  quarantined unread and later deleted on the owner's approval (J-0007,
  J-0008, D-014, D-016).
\item
  \textbf{Reports.} The experiment reports were composed from committed
  results only and written to disk by the coordinating session, on the
  owner's approval (D-020).
\end{itemize}

\subsection{5. Results}\label{results}

All results are from synthetic simulations. Unless marked exploratory,
they come from the frozen analyses of the committed outputs in
\texttt{results/confirmatory/}. No run was invalid, excluded, dropped or
retried: 810 of 810 runs for EXP-001, 810 of 810 for EXP-002 and 1,440
of 1,440 for EXP-003.

The pooled POPULARITY effect hides heterogeneity across cells (Table 3,

Secondary metrics (descriptive, no tests;
\texttt{EXP-001\_arm\_summary.csv}) show that POPULARITY had higher
mutual satisfaction M than RANDOM in all nine cells and fewer blocking
pairs per 100 agents in all nine cells. It left fewer agents unmatched
than RANDOM in all three balanced cells and more in the two cells where
its welfare effect was negative. Its exposure Gini on side B was higher
than RANDOM's in six cells. EXPOSURE\_BALANCED did not consistently
equalize exposure: its side-B exposure Gini was higher than RANDOM's in

most 1.05\% of its slates in any cell. On timing, EXPOSURE\_BALANCED
resembled RANDOM rather than POPULARITY: its share of short slates
(fewer than five unseen candidates left) was 0.0649 to 0.4910 per cell,
against 0.0822 to 0.5325 for RANDOM and 0 for POPULARITY, and like
RANDOM it stopped forming matches early (Section 5.4).

\subsubsection{5.4 Exploratory diagnostics (M4; not
confirmatory)}\label{exploratory-diagnostics-m4-not-confirmatory}

\textbf{E1, horizon saturation.} In the committed EXP-001 runs, every
POPULARITY instance formed between 2 and 7 matches in round 40, the last
round, and on average 25.2\% to 26.8\% of its matches per cell formed in
the last 10 rounds
(\texttt{results/exploratory/m4\_confounders/horizon\_saturation.csv}).
RANDOM and EXPOSURE\_BALANCED had stopped forming matches before round
31 in every instance except in the r = 1.5 cells with rho \textgreater{}
0 (RANDOM: 57\% of instances at rho = 0.9; EXPOSURE\_BALANCED: 3\% and
7\%). The primary T = 40 outcome is therefore close to final for the
comparator but truncated for POPULARITY.

\textbf{E4, horizon-extension probe.} On a fresh exploratory seed with
10 instances per cell
(\texttt{results/exploratory/m4\_horizon\_probe/analysis/pooled.csv}),
the POPULARITY contrast was +0.0217 (95\% CI +0.0196 to +0.0238) at T =
40, close to the confirmatory value, and +0.0375 (+0.0356 to +0.0394) at
T = 80. It was identical at T = 160 because no arm formed a match after
round 60. At T = 40 POPULARITY left slightly more agents unmatched than
RANDOM (equal-weight Delta U +0.0026); at T = 80 it left fewer
(-0.0199). At T = 80 the POPULARITY effect was positive in all nine
cells, including the two cells that were negative at T = 40 (+0.0328 at
r = 1.5, rho = 0.5 and +0.0195 at r = 1.5, rho = 0.9). The last
POPULARITY match came at round 40 in every balanced instance, by round
44 at r = 1.1 and by round 60 at r = 1.5, which equals the number of
rounds needed to show all 200, 220 or 300 long-side candidates five at a
time. This bound is mechanical: since no candidate is shown twice to the
same viewer, under any policy a viewer has seen the whole other side
after at most that many rounds. The EXPOSURE\_BALANCED contrast, +0.0022
(+0.0002 to +0.0041), did not change with the horizon.

\textbf{E2, unmatched-value sweep.} Valuing an unmatched agent at any
constant v between 0 and 1 moves the EXP-001 POPULARITY contrast from
+0.0219 to +0.0239 and the EXPOSURE\_BALANCED contrast from +0.0004 to
+0.0043, whose 90\% CI stays within (-0.01, 0.01) for every v in the
grid (\texttt{unmatched\_value\_sweep.csv}). The S2 reversals are more
sensitive: the POPULARITY contrast at T = 10 would change sign at v =
0.75 and at T = 20 at v = 0.72; at v = 0.5 it remains negative (-0.1349
and -0.0868).

\textbf{E3, decomposition.} In EXP-001, POPULARITY matched a slightly
smaller share of agents than RANDOM (-0.0020 on the equal-weight scale)
but its matched agents had a higher mean satisfaction (+0.0282, 95\% CI
+0.0272 to +0.0292). At T = 10 the gain in the mean satisfaction of
matched agents was the same (+0.0282) while the matched share fell by
0.5463 (\texttt{decomposition.csv}). Q is an average over whichever
agents are matched, so these differences mix partner quality with the
composition of the matched set.

\subsection{6. Discussion}\label{discussion}

\textbf{What the confirmatory result says.} Within this model, at 40
rounds and the primary pickiness, popularity-ranked slates gave a higher
equal-weight mean welfare than random slates, and exposure-balanced
slates gave a welfare equivalent to random slates within 0.01. The
registered sensitivity analysis then showed that the popularity effect
depends on the horizon: at 10 and 20 rounds popularity ranking is far
worse than random exposure, because most agents are still unmatched.

\textbf{Mechanism suggested by the evidence.} The decomposition (E3) and
the secondary metrics agree on one reading. Popularity ranking slows the
formation of matches, and the agents it does match are, on average, more
satisfied. The mean satisfaction of matched agents is higher under
POPULARITY in every setting examined, and mutual satisfaction is higher
in every cell. These are averages over the matched agents, so part of
the difference may come from which agents are matched rather than from
better partners for the same agents; the design cannot separate the two.
What changes across horizons and cells is how many agents are matched by
the end. POPULARITY keeps forming matches until viewers have seen the
entire other side, whereas RANDOM stops far earlier. One explanation is
that, with the shared per-round tie key and identical initial scores,
viewers see nearly the same slates, as observed in the pre-freeze pilot
(J-0003), so mutual likes form late. This is a hypothesis resting on
that exploratory observation; it was not tested. If the eventual
allocation is what matters, the horizon-extension probe suggests that
POPULARITY matches both more agents and more satisfied agents than
RANDOM once both have stopped, but that probe is exploratory (10
instances per cell, a new seed, designed after the S2 result) and serves
only to motivate a pre-registered horizon-free experiment.

\textbf{Competing explanations.} Table 6 lists the competing
explanations named in the frozen protocols and what the evidence says
about each.

\textbf{Implications.} Within the model, the comparison between ranking
policies cannot be separated from the question of how long participants
search, measured relative to the rounds needed to see the other side
(n\_B / k, here 40 to 60 rounds); the study used one market size and one
slate length, so these horizons do not transfer to other sizes or to
real search durations. In this model, a policy that sorts candidates by
one shared score slowed the formation of matches, while the agents it
matched were on average more satisfied. Exposure-balanced ranking, by
contrast, behaved much like random exposure on timing and exposure
inequality, which may explain why its welfare did not differ from random
exposure. Whether this trade-off is favourable depends on how long
agents search, on how being unmatched is valued, and on market
imbalance. The magnitudes matter as much as the signs: the confirmatory
POPULARITY gain (0.0219) is about a quarter of the gap between deferred
acceptance and random discovery (0.0963). The centralized references
show the size of the gap left by sequential discovery: deferred
acceptance exceeded random discovery by about 0.10 in welfare, and the
welfare-maximizing assignment reached higher welfare still, at the price
of many blocking pairs. In that limited sense, the working question
``can optimal matching leave more people unhappy?'' has a two-sided
answer here: the welfare-optimal assignment leaves many pairs who would
rather deviate, yet its mean welfare is the highest of all arms.

\textbf{Relation to prior work.} The finding that a relevance-sorted
policy can be much worse than random exposure at horizons well below
n\_B / k is not in conflict with the argument of Su et al.~(2021) that
relevance ranking is suboptimal under capacity constraints, but the
settings, objectives and policies differ and no direct comparison is
possible. The strong short-side advantage under deferred acceptance with
imbalance is consistent with the abstract of Ashlagi et al.~(2017),
which concerns stable matchings in random markets.

\subsection{7. Limitations and threats to
validity}\label{limitations-and-threats-to-validity}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Synthetic model.} Utilities are Gaussian
  common-plus-idiosyncratic draws; agents like a candidate exactly when
  utility exceeds a fixed quantile; there is no strategy, learning,
  fatigue, messaging or exit. A single market size (200 agents on the
  short side) was studied. Nothing here can be read as evidence about
  real people, real dating or job platforms, or any proprietary ranking
  system.
\item
  \textbf{Horizon.} The primary horizon T = 40 was chosen by the owner
  after exploratory values were seen (C4); it is the horizon at which
  POPULARITY had turned positive in the pilot, and it equals n\_B / k in
  the balanced cells. Its stated purpose, letting all arms stop
  matching, was not achieved for POPULARITY when r \textgreater{} 1. The
  registered sensitivity analysis showed that the POPULARITY sign
  depends on T, and exploratory diagnostics indicate that T = 40
  truncates POPULARITY but not RANDOM. The confirmatory p-value is valid
  for the registered fixed-horizon contrast; it is not evidence for a
  horizon-free or final-allocation effect. Horizons are meaningful only
  relative to n\_B / k in this model.
\item
  \textbf{Metric definition.} The registered metric-definition check
  (S3) was not run. The exploratory unmatched-value sweep covers only
  one part of it.
\item
  \textbf{Policy implementation.} POPULARITY uses one shared random tie
  key per round. In the pre-freeze exploratory runs at T = 20, the
  POPULARITY contrast was -0.2917 with the shared key (nine cells,
  J-0003) and -0.0422 with per-viewer keys (corner cells, J-0005). The
  results describe this implementation, not popularity ranking in
  general.
\item
  \textbf{EXPOSURE\_BALANCED construct.} The cap limits per-round
  exposure relative to the popularity order; it did not produce lower
  exposure inequality than random exposure in four of nine cells, and
  its timing resembled random exposure. Its equivalence result is a
  result about this cap rule, which behaved much like random exposure,
  not about exposure balancing as a goal.
\item
  \textbf{Estimand.} theta\_P is an equal-weight average over nine
  chosen cells; the POPULARITY sign varies across cells at T = 40, so
  another cell mix would give a different value.
\item
  \textbf{Statistics.} The intervals quantify only sampling variation
  across synthetic instances within one model; they are narrow because
  of common random numbers and say nothing about model uncertainty. The
  p-value is floored by the number of draws. Per-cell CIs and EXP-002
  and EXP-003 contrasts are not multiplicity-protected.
\item
  \textbf{Information confound.} The centralized arms use full
  preferences; the EXP-002 welfare contrast mixes information and
  mechanism.
\item
  \textbf{Literature.} The review was short and non-systematic; several
  sources were verified only at metadata or abstract level.
\item
  \textbf{Runtime.} Runs shared a machine with other work; runtimes are
  diagnostics only.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{8. Ethics and responsible
research}\label{ethics-and-responsible-research}

All data are generated by code from recorded seeds; no dataset of real
people was used, downloaded or redistributed, and public speed-dating
and ratings datasets were examined only to record why they are excluded
(\texttt{research/literature\_review.md}). Subgroups are sides and
synthetic quality quartiles, never protected attributes. No ethics
approval was sought because no human participant was involved; none is
claimed. The results must not be used to describe or rank real people,
to infer protected attributes, or to make claims about how any real
platform ranks users.

\subsection{9. Conclusion and future
work}\label{conclusion-and-future-work}

In synthetic two-sided markets with reciprocal preferences,
popularity-ranked slates raised mean welfare relative to random slates
after 40 rounds, but the sign of this effect reverses at shorter
horizons, so under the frozen rule it is not robust. Exposure-balanced
slates were equivalent to random slates within 0.01. Deferred acceptance
clearly exceeded random discovery, and the welfare-maximizing assignment
left many more blocking pairs than deferred acceptance. Exploratory
diagnostics suggest that popularity ranking matches agents more slowly,
that the agents it matches are on average more satisfied, and that the
primary horizon truncated it; whether its eventual allocation is better
is a hypothesis for a pre-registered horizon-free experiment, not a
finding. Feasible next steps are a pre-registered horizon-free outcome
(welfare once no new match can form), a fully specified
metric-definition sensitivity with matchings retained in the raw
outputs, a per-viewer tie-key arm, and a sequential arm with full
information to separate information from mechanism.

\subsection{10. Data, code availability and artifact
reproducibility}\label{data-code-availability-and-artifact-reproducibility}

All code, configurations, raw results, analysis tables and figures are
in the project repository (public URL: to be added after the owner's
approval). The environment is installed with
\texttt{uv\ sync\ -\/-frozen}. The confirmatory runs are reproduced with
\texttt{python\ -m\ match\_lab\ run\ -\/-config\ experiments/configs/EXP-00N.json}
(N = 1, 2, 3) in a clean clone, the frozen tables with
\texttt{python\ -m\ match\_lab\ report\ ...} and
\texttt{python\ -m\ match\_lab\ analyze\ ...}, and the exploratory
diagnostics with the scripts in \texttt{experiments/exploratory/}. Exact
commands, hashes and checksums are in each experiment's
\texttt{reproduction.md}, and the mapping from every number to its
source is in \texttt{research/publication/artifact\_manifest.json}.
Metrics are deterministic given configuration and seed; the analysis
draws use fixed seeds.
